summary: Specifies the protocol an IPv6 router uses to discover which neighboring nodes want to receive multicast packets, and which multicast addresses they are interested in. It is the IPv6 counterpart of IGMP. It is a standards-track protocol at the proposed standard level.

plainLanguage.summary: Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) lets an IPv6 router learn which multicast addresses devices want to receive. The router shares that information with its multicast routing component so packets can reach the links where listeners are present.

questions: how does ipv6 multicast membership work
how does mld differ from igmp
subtitle: How IPv6 routers learn which multicast addresses have listeners on each attached link.

tldr.problem: An IPv6 router needs to know which multicast addresses have interested listeners on each directly attached link. This lets multicast routing send packets only to links where receivers are present.
tldr.mechanism: Routers send Queries, listeners answer with Reports after a random delay, and a listener can send Done when it stops listening. Routers keep a timer for each address and update their multicast routing component when listener presence changes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2710 specifies MLD as a Proposed Standard derived from IGMPv2. It has been updated by RFC 3590, RFC 3810 and RFC 9777.

today: RFC 2710 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 3590, RFC 3810 and RFC 9777.

sections.title: What MLD Helps Routers Learn
sections.content:
Multicast Listener Discovery (MLD) tells an IPv6 router whether nodes on a directly attached link want multicast traffic, and which multicast addresses they want. The router passes this information to its multicast routing protocol so traffic can reach links with interested receivers.

MLD follows the design of IPv4's Internet Group Management Protocol version 2 (IGMPv2), but it uses ICMPv6 message types. A router that listens to a multicast address also performs the listener role for that address.

Listeners run MLD on every interface where an application or upper-layer protocol requested multicast reception. A router with multiple interfaces to the same link runs the router role on only one of them.
sections.plainLanguage: MLD tells an IPv6 router which multicast groups have listeners on a nearby link. The router uses that information to decide where multicast packets need to go.

sections.title: The Three MLD Messages
sections.content:
MLD messages are part of Internet Control Message Protocol for IPv6 (ICMPv6). Each message has a 24-octet format and carries a multicast address. The three message types are Query (130), Report (131) and Done (132).

A Query asks about listeners. A zero multicast-address field means a General Query about all relevant groups; a named address means a query about that group. A Report names an address the sender is listening to, and a Done names an address the sender is leaving.

MLD packets use a link-local IPv6 source address, a Hop Limit of 1 and the IPv6 Router Alert option. A sender must not send a message longer than 24 octets. A receiver ignores bytes after that limit, but the checksum covers the whole message.
sections.plainLanguage: A Query asks which groups have listeners. A Report names a group the sender wants, and Done names a group the sender has left.

sections.title: Queries, Reports and Listener Timers
sections.content:
On each link, routers choose one Querier. All routers start in that role; a router that hears a Query from a lower IPv6 source address becomes a Non-Querier. It can become Querier again after the Other Querier Present Interval passes without hearing from a lower-address router.

The Querier periodically sends a General Query to the all-nodes address, FF02::1. A listener starts a separate random response timer for each relevant group. When a timer expires, the listener sends a Report. If it first hears another listener report the same group, it cancels its timer and stays silent, reducing duplicate Reports.

The router records whether each group has listeners on the link and refreshes that group's timer when it receives a Report. When a listener leaves, it SHOULD send Done to FF02::2. The Querier then sends group-specific Queries; if no Report arrives, it removes the group from its list and informs the multicast routing component.
sections.plainLanguage: The Querier asks about groups on a schedule. Listeners wait for a random time before replying, and a listener can stay quiet if another device has already reported the same group.

sections.title: Listener and Router States
sections.content:
For each group on each interface, a node is a Non-Listener, a Delaying Listener with a response timer running, or an Idle Listener with no response timer running. Starting to listen moves the node out of Non-Listener; a query can make an Idle Listener start a timer; stopping listening returns it to Non-Listener.

A router separately tracks whether it is Querier or Non-Querier on a link. For each group, it can have No Listeners Present, Listeners Present or Checking Listeners state. Checking Listeners begins after a Done and continues through the last-listener query procedure, even if the router changes from Querier to Non-Querier during that procedure.

The link-scope all-nodes address, FF02::1, is a special case. A node remains an Idle Listener for it and never sends a Report or Done for that address.
sections.plainLanguage: A listening device is either waiting to report or has no report timer running. A router tracks whether each group has listeners and whether a leaving listener still needs to be checked.

sections.title: Timer Defaults
sections.content:
Most MLD timers can be configured, but non-default settings must be consistent among routers on one link. The Robustness Variable defaults to 2 and tunes the protocol for expected packet loss. It must not be zero and SHOULD NOT be one.

The Query Interval defaults to 125 seconds. The Query Response Interval defaults to 10000 milliseconds and must be less than the Query Interval. The Last Listener Query Interval defaults to 1000 milliseconds, and the Unsolicited Report Interval defaults to 10 seconds.

The Multicast Listener Interval determines how long a router waits before deciding that a group has no listeners. The RFC requires it to equal the Robustness Variable multiplied by the Query Interval, plus one Query Response Interval.
sections.plainLanguage: Timers control how often the router asks, how long listeners may wait to answer, and when the router decides a group has no listeners. Routers on one link need consistent timer settings.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MLD nodes check that received messages use a link-local IPv6 source address. The RFC therefore focuses on forged messages sent by a machine on the same link.

A forged Query can make the attacker appear to be Querier. If it then stops sending Queries and ignores Done messages, traffic for groups without listeners may continue for up to the Multicast Listener Interval. A forged Report can make a router believe a group has listeners, while a forged Done causes extra group-specific Queries but cannot remove desired traffic.

A forged Query can also make listeners send extra Reports. The RFC says that this causes some additional link traffic but no protocol problem.
sections.plainLanguage: A device on the same link can send false MLD messages. These can cause extra queries or keep traffic flowing after listeners leave, but a false Done does not stop wanted traffic.

fields.name: Code
fields.desc: Zero when sent; ignored when received.

fields.name: Checksum
fields.desc: ICMPv6 checksum over the whole message and pseudo-header.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Zero when sent; ignored when received.

fields.name: Multicast Address
fields.desc: Zero in a General Query; otherwise the group address.

items.label: Query Response Interval
items.desc: Default maximum response delay in General Queries.

items.label: Unsolicited Report Interval
items.desc: Default interval between repeated initial Reports.
